records.found: Nothing dated 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-09 meets the test: the hepatitis B trial's registry entry (NCT06671093) is unchanged since 2026-01-06, still recruiting, with no posted results and no peer-reviewed report. Scribe Therapeutics announced it would present updated data at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions on 2026-11-07; a news summary of the release says one dose of STX-1150 held LDL cholesterol down for at least two years in monkeys. Animal data, not human results. The wire copy of the release refused to open; the summary page was opened.
The company release itself (GlobeNewswire), seen only as a search listing; the page returned an access refusal.

Peer-reviewed paper in Cell Stem Cell (Ye and colleagues): editors that rewrite DNA marks silenced a platelet gene in human blood-forming stem cells in the laboratory, and the silencing held four months after the cells were transplanted into mice. Human cells, not a treated person; does not meet the first-human test.

records.found: No published uptake figure and no regulator decision appeared between 2026-11-02 and 2026-11-09, so the wide-use test is not met. Dated in the window are a trade-press report of 2026-11-03 that a different amyloid antibody, sabirnetug, lowered amyloid on scans but did not slow decline in a 542-person trial and was dropped (the company's announcement was on 2026-10-30, three days before the window); a German paper of 2026-11-06 recording that the national assessment found no added benefit for donanemab; Singapore use recommendations for lecanemab published 2026-11-04; and a 3,000-person study of real-world use in China first registered on 2026-11-06.

findings.what: NeurologyLive report dated 2026-11-03 on Acumen Pharmaceuticals' announcement of 2026-10-30: in the 542-person ALTITUDE-AD trial in early Alzheimer's disease, neither dose of the amyloid antibody sabirnetug differed from placebo on the main 18-month measure of thinking and function, and the key secondary measures were not met, although scans showed a dose-related fall in amyloid; about one in ten treated people had brain swelling on scans; the company is stopping development. A counter-example to the entry's test: amyloid lowered without slower decline. The underlying announcement is dated just before the window.

Paper in a German journal (Fortschritte der Neurologie Psychiatrie): donanemab has been available since 2025, but Germany's added-benefit assessment, which informs the price, recognised no added benefit in either stage of early Alzheimer's disease, in contrast with the European marketing authorisation. Bears against wide use in Germany.

Paper in Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore: appropriate-use recommendations for lecanemab, which the abstract says has been approved in Singapore. One more country where it can be prescribed; no uptake figure.

Registry entry first posted 2026-11-06: Fudan University's multi-centre look-back study of the safety and effectiveness of disease-modifying Alzheimer's treatment in routine care in China, estimated 3,000 people, started 2026-10-26. A sign of the scale of use in China; a registration, not a figure.

Just before the window: Eisai's preliminary revenue notice for lecanemab for 2026-04-01 to 2026-09-30: 61.5 billion yen worldwide (41.1 billion a year earlier), of which 32.5 billion in the United States, 13.0 billion in Japan and 9.7 billion in China. It gives no count of people treated, so the record's point that sales are published but uptake is not still stands.

Just before the window: Eisai's notice that it will present five-year lecanemab data and real-world research at an Alzheimer's trials conference (seen on Eisai's news list; the release itself not opened).

records.found: The window's records point towards use widening, which supports the estimate's likely year of 2030 or a little earlier: Pfizer's filing of 2026-11-03 reports tafamidis sales of $1,773 million for the quarter, up 12 per cent, on a growing United States market, more diagnoses abroad and lower net prices under new insurer contracts, which is the mechanism the estimate relies on, and a Circulation paper of the same day shows a competing gene silencer still cutting deaths at four years. Against that, no share of eligible people treated was published, and a United States claims study of 2026-11-04 found a median of 5.2 years from first sign to diagnosis, so many eligible people are still not found. The entry also lacks an older result against the class: on 2026-07-09 AstraZeneca reported that the gene silencer eplontersen did not meet its main measure in a late-stage heart trial.

findings.what: Pfizer's quarterly report filed 2026-11-03 for the quarter ended 2026-09-27: the tafamidis family brought in $1,773 million worldwide ($1,591 million a year earlier), $1,086 million of it in the United States and $687 million abroad; $5,136 million over nine months. The filing attributes growth to continued market expansion in the United States, continuing uptake in patient diagnosis and improved access in international markets, partly offset over the nine months by net price erosion in the United States from new payer contracts. Sales, not a count of people treated.

Peer-reviewed paper in Circulation: one-year results of the open-label extension of the HELIOS-B trial of the gene silencer vutrisiran, followed to month 48. Of 654 original participants 466 entered the extension; those on the drug throughout had a 37 per cent lower risk of death from any cause, and of a first heart event or death, than those who began on placebo. A second kind of drug in the entry's class holding its effect on deaths over four years.

Peer-reviewed paper in Clinical Research in Cardiology on early routine use in Germany of acoramidis, the second protein-steadying pill (approved in the European Union in February 2025): 289 people had it dispensed between April and September 2025 in a prescription database covering 82 per cent of reimbursed prescriptions; median age 82; 86 per cent had not been on tafamidis before. A published uptake count for a competitor, though small and for one country.

Peer-reviewed paper in the Journal of the American Heart Association: in United States insurance claims for 7,509 people (mean age 75.9), the median time from the first recorded sign to diagnosis of the heart condition was 5.2 years. Late diagnosis limits the share of eligible people who can be on the drug.

Intellia's third-quarter release of 2026-11-05 (filed copy on sec.gov): enrolment in the late-stage heart trial of its one-time gene editor nex-z has advanced, and enrolment in the companion nerve-disease trial was completed in the third quarter. No results and no new safety stop reported.

Older fact the entry lacks: AstraZeneca's stock-exchange notice of 2026-07-09 that the late-stage CARDIO-TTRansform trial of the gene silencer eplontersen in this heart condition did not meet its main measure (heart deaths and repeat heart events to 140 weeks against placebo), in people most of whom were already on a protein-steadying pill. The estimate lists gene silencers among the arriving competitors; this one failed on top of standard care. No mention of eplontersen was found in the records.

Just before the window: BridgeBio's third-quarter release of 2026-10-29 (filed copy on sec.gov) reports $253.2 million of United States sales of acoramidis in the quarter, about $145 million more than a year earlier, with growth led by newly diagnosed people starting treatment. Sales, not a share of eligible people.

Registry updates in the window with no posted change of substance, seen in the dated listing only: the eplontersen extension study (NCT06194825, updated 2026-11-06), HELIOS-B (NCT04153149, updated 2026-11-02, results first posted 2025-10-21) and the nex-z heart trial MAGNITUDE (NCT06128629, updated 2026-11-04, recruiting).
